name: Fallacy of four terms
statement: A categorical syllogism must contain exactly three terms, and one that smuggles in a fourth, usually by letting a word change sense, proves nothing.
meaning: Copi's first rule for the categorical syllogism is that it must contain exactly three terms, each of which is used in the same sense throughout the argument. Break the rule and the premises never relate the two end terms to one third thing, so the conclusion rests on nothing. There are two ways to break it. The fourth term can be printed, as when four class names appear and the reader does not count them. More often it is hidden. One word occurs in both premises with a different sense in each, so the argument has three terms in sound and four in meaning. Copi's example is a defence of Japanese activity in China circulated in the late 1930s. For its first premise to be accepted, 'attempts to end hostilities' has to mean proposing an armistice and negotiating in good faith. For its second to be true, the phrase has to cover the vigorous prosecution of war. Whately drew the same line a century earlier without the Latin name. His formulation of the hidden case is that if the middle term is ambiguous there are in reality two middle terms, in sense, though but one in sound. Copi adds a footnote saying the same name is applied to the fallacy even where the argument contains as many as five or six different terms.

origin.note: The year of the textbook that carries the English name, not of the idea. Copi's Rule 1 for standard form categorical syllogisms reads that a valid one must contain exactly three terms, each used in the same sense throughout the argument. The text names a violation of it the Fallacy of Four Terms, in Latin Quaternio Terminorum. The Latin is older than the book and how much older was not traced here. Richard Whately's Elements of Logic, read in the 1845 Boston edition, already separates arguments with palpably more than three terms from those with an ambiguous middle, and uses neither the Latin nor the English name. The first edition of 1953 was read as a scanned copy at the Internet Archive; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy describes the classification in the 1961 second edition, which was not obtained.

evidence: One experimental programme has put four-term arguments to people, and it is the Cagliari work the Atlas records under equivocation. Ervas and colleagues built arguments in Italian whose middle term shifted sense between the premises, which is the hidden form of the fallacy, and crossed that with the kind of word doing the shifting. Their names for the three argument structures show what was being tested: a strong argument holding the sense fixed, a standard quaternio terminorum whose conclusion is plainly false, and a quaternio terminorum whose conclusion is plausible. Experiment 1 tested 147 adults recruited at the University of Cagliari, none of whom had taken a course in logic or argumentation theory, and excluded 19 for failing the fillers. Accuracy fell furthest in the plausible-conclusion condition, and response times moved with it. The main effect of argument structure on response time was F(2,144) = 3.94, p = 0.02, and participants took longer over a quaternio terminorum with a plausible conclusion than over a strong argument, t(145) = 4.07, p < 0.001. Experiment 2 put 24 of those plausible-conclusion arguments and 24 fillers to 50 participants through an online form, with the same yes-or-no question and seven rating scales attached. Understandability and belief in the conclusion predicted accepting the argument in every middle-term condition, belief running to t(48) = 3.7, p < 0.001 for homonymous middle terms. The acceptance rates belong to the equivocation entry and are not repeated here; they were re-read from the article for this entry and matched. The classical syllogism task says nothing about this fallacy. Its 64 pairs of premises are built from a middle term and two end terms, so a fourth term cannot arise in them. The strings 'four terms' and 'equivocation' do not occur in the text of Khemlani and Johnson-Laird's meta-analysis of that task.

replication.headline: Two experiments with different samples and different tasks agree that people accept a syllogism whose fourth term is hidden by a shift of sense, and the whole record comes from one group in one city.
replication.detail: Experiment 1 measured accuracy and response time on 147 participants in the laboratory. Experiment 2 measured acceptance on 50 participants online, using a subset of the same items and adding rating scales, and the paper states that its results confirmed the first experiment's on the yes-or-no question. The direction that holds across both is not about ambiguity. The same shifting words drew far fewer correct answers once the conclusion was made plausible rather than plainly false. Belief in the conclusion predicted acceptance in every condition. That is the shape of belief bias rather than of a blindness to sense. The Atlas records a 2021 follow-up from an overlapping team on the equivocation entry, with its figures; it was not obtained for this entry. No independent test was located. Semantic Scholar lists 18 papers citing the 2018 article and none of them repeats the experiment.

study.cite: Ervas, F., Ledda, A., Ojha, A., Pierro, G. A., & Indurkhya, B. (2018). Creative Argumentation: When and Why People Commit the Metaphoric Fallacy. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 1815.

limits: The measured half of this entry covers the hidden fourth term only. The printed case, where a syllogism carries four plainly different class names, has no experiment located. The search covered Europe PMC. There 'quaternio terminorum' returns two records and both are the Cagliari papers, while 'fallacy of four terms' and 'four-term fallacy' return none. A search on 'four terms' with syllogism returns those two papers and an 1862 notice about medical degrees. Crossref's bibliographic search on quaternio terminorum returns work on Kant, on Jung and on dictionary headwords. Van Eemeren, Garssen and Meuffels tested how ordinary people judge violations of the pragma-dialectical discussion rules. Crossref lists chapters of that book on the freedom rule, the obligation to defend, the argument scheme rule and the concluding rule. None of the chapters it lists is on the rule about clear language. The experiments that do exist ran in Italian on students at one university, with arguments on a screen and a yes-or-no question, which is not an argument anyone is pressing in earnest. Neither paper reports a standardised effect size for the acceptance result, so this entry's effect-size fields are empty. One comparison in Experiment 1 is printed as t(145) = -1.39, p = 1.01, and a probability above one cannot be read, so nothing is taken from it here. Experiment 2 states fifty participants and lists 31 women, 8 men and 1 other. Copi and Whately were read as scanned page images turned into text, so wording is quoted from the scan and no page number is quoted from it.
misreadings: The commonest error is to think counting terms settles the question. Copi's own text warns that a syllogism whose propositions appear to involve more than three terms is not to be rejected out of hand. It gives one that is valid: all mammals are warm-blooded animals, no lizards are warm-blooded animals, therefore all lizards are non-mammals. It has four terms and translates into a standard form syllogism, because one term is the complement of another, and the reductions are done by conversion, obversion and contraposition. A second error is to file the fallacy under one heading. Copi's 1953 text discusses equivocation among the informal fallacies of ambiguity and the four-terms rule among the rules for syllogisms, so the same error appears twice in one book. The Stanford Encyclopedia records that Copi's classification lists the fallacy of four terms among the formal fallacies while equivocation sits among the informal ones. Whately's version of the division is the useful one. Cases with palpably more than three terms are purely logical, and the ambiguous middle is semi-logical. Finding the ambiguity needs attention to the sense of the term and knowledge of the subject matter, so logic teaches us not how to find the fallacy but only where to search for it. A third error confuses this with the undistributed middle, which the Atlas covers separately. There the middle term keeps one sense and the premises fail to speak about the same members of it. Whately puts that case under the purely logical head because the fault shows in the form. A fourth error reads the Cagliari results as evidence that people cannot see ambiguity. What moved the answers was how believable the conclusion was.

sources.text: Copi, I. M. (1953). Introduction to Logic. New York: The Macmillan Company. Read as the Internet Archive scan of the seventh printing, downloaded twice and checked against the title page for the author's name. Source for Rule 1, for the naming of the Fallacy of Four Terms and Quaternio Terminorum, for the footnote about five or six terms, for the 1930s example about China, for the valid four-term syllogism about lizards, and for the placement of equivocation among the fallacies of ambiguity.

Whately, R. (1845). Elements of Logic. Boston: James Munroe and Company. Read as the Internet Archive scan of the stereotype edition, downloaded twice. Source for the division of purely logical from semi-logical fallacies, for the sentence that an ambiguous middle term makes two middle terms in sense though but one in sound, and for the remark that logic teaches us not how to find the fallacy but only where to search for it.

Hansen, H. Fallacies. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Read as the raw page. Source for the statement that Copi's classification places the fallacy of four terms among the formal fallacies, alongside affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent, undistributed middle and illicit major, and equivocation among the informal fallacies of ambiguity.

Ervas, F., Ledda, A., Ojha, A., Pierro, G. A., & Indurkhya, B. (2018). Creative Argumentation: When and Why People Commit the Metaphoric Fallacy. Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 1815. Read as the JATS XML from PubMed Central, PMC6168032, fetched twice to the same checksum. Source for the design, the samples, the response-time results and the Experiment 2 predictors quoted above, and for the definition of quaternio terminorum as a fallacious argument based on the lexical ambiguity of its middle term.

Ervas, F., Rossi, M. G., Ojha, A., & Indurkhya, B. (2021). The Double Framing Effect of Emotive Metaphors in Argumentation. Frontiers in Psychology, 12, 628460. Named as the later study from an overlapping team; not obtained for this entry, and its figures are quoted on the Atlas entry for equivocation.

Khemlani, S., & Johnson-Laird, P. N. (2012). Theories of the syllogism: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 138(3), 427-457. Read as the PDF at modeltheory.org and searched in full. Source for the statement that the 64 pairs of premises are built from a middle term and two end terms.

van Eemeren, F. H., Garssen, B., & Meuffels, B. (2009). Fallacies and Judgments of Reasonableness. Dordrecht: Springer. Named as the place an experiment on judging this fallacy would sit; the chapter list at Crossref was checked and the book was not obtained.
